description: We are a multidisciplinary team passionate about physics, mathematics, AI, and emerging technologies. Our project explores planetary science through machine learning, geospatial analysis, and advanced computational methods. We seek members skilled in Python, machine learning, data management, GIS, remote sensing, geology, and scientific research. Curiosity, creativity, and collaborative problem-solving are essential.
summary:
QuantumAnalog is an open, reproducible planetary science tool that evaluates and explains how closely any terrestrial region resembles specific target sites on Mars or the Moon.

What we developed:
We standardized elevation and surface data across Earth, Mars, and Moon to a common grid, describing every location using six core physical features: slope, roughness, local relief, relative elevation, curvature, and albedo. We then built a similarity matching pipeline using classical machine learning kernels and a quantum fidelity kernel powered by six qubits.

How it addresses the challenge:
The project tackles the NASA Space Apps Challenge by identifying new terrestrial analog sites, quantifying their similarity, and pinpointing exact feature mismatches using leave-one-feature-out attribution. We benchmarked the pipeline against Death Valley and mapped Kharan-Chagai, Pakistan, against 14 Martian and lunar reference sites, visualized via an interactive web app.

Why it matters:
This proof-of-concept establishes a highly generalizable framework for planetary site selection. By requiring only Earth data and target planetary data, the model can evaluate any region on Earth—in any country—against Martian or lunar targets using quantum kernels. When fully developed, it will provide NASA with a precise, primary data-based classification tool to identify ideal terrestrial test sites worldwide, with future iterations poised to fully leverage advanced quantum advantages.
details:
Project Details

Overview & Repository Reference For judges and reviewers looking for complete technical specifications, environment setup instructions, and code execution guidelines, please consult the repository README.md. Furthermore, an extensive, formal academic paper detailing the theoretical framework, mathematical formulations, data pipelines, and full experimental results is available in the repository under docs/QuantumAnalog_paper.pdf.

1. What does your project do, and how does it work?
Our model is a proof of concept that compares Earth locations with the surface of Mars and the Moon to find analogs. We validated it with a benchmark test on Death Valley, then applied it to a new region, for example, the Chagai area of Balochistan, Pakistan, whose features closely resemble those of the Martian sites.

QuantumAnalog is an open, reproducible planetary science tool that scores how closely any terrestrial region resembles a chosen site on Mars or the Moon, and provides complete explainability for its matches.

  • Data Standardization & Grid: Elevation and surface data across Earth, Mars, and the Moon are resampled to a common 1.9 km ground pixel using correct planetary radii. Regions are analyzed across a mesh of 5.7 km cells (3 x 3 pixel neighborhoods) inspired by fluid dynamics.
  • The Six Surface Features: Every cell is described by the exact same six physical numbers: slope, roughness (detrended RMS elevation scatter), local relief (max z - min z), relative elevation (z - mean z), curvature (negative Laplacian), and albedo.
  • Similarity Kernels: The tool utilizes classical machine learning kernels (Linear, Polynomial, RBF, Laplacian) and a quantum fidelity kernel (angle embedding and IQP entanglement embedding across 6 qubits) as precision similarity meters.
  • Explainability Pipeline: A leave-one-feature-out attribution test calculates mismatch scores for every match, identifying precisely which physical features support or break an analogy (such as explaining why the dry lake bed Hamun-i-Mashkel matches Meridiani Planum terrain despite brightness/albedo differences).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Universal Applicability: By requiring only Earth data and target planetary data, the model can be expanded to evaluate any region on Earth—in any country—against Martian or lunar targets.
  • Interpretable Analog Selection: Unlike black-box tools, QuantumAnalog breaks down analogies feature-by-feature with clear anomaly attribution.
  • Robust Prototyping & Reproducibility: Features a modular repository architecture split between a synthetic prototype (prototype_synthetic/) and the real NASA data model (QuantumAnalog/), complete with an interactive Streamlit application (app.py) and hardware simulation workflows (step6_hardware.py).

3. What is the intended impact of the project? When fully scaled to its maximum capacity, QuantumAnalog serves as a primary data-based classification tool for space agencies like NASA. If researchers want to determine which physical locations on Earth are optimal for testing rovers, life-detection instruments, or habitat prototypes under Martian or lunar conditions, this model can accurately identify and rank candidate terrestrial test sites worldwide using free NASA data. While this proof-of-concept establishes a powerful baseline, future iterations aim to expand global coverage with high-performance computing, integrate advanced surface features (thermal inertia, mineralogy, rock abundance, subsurface properties), and fully leverage emerging quantum hardware advantages and trained quantum embeddings as quantum technology matures.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages & Core Frameworks: Python 3.12, scikit-learn (SVM and classical kernels), NumPy, SciPy, pandas, h5py, Matplotlib.
  • Quantum Computing Libraries: PennyLane (quantum kernels), Qiskit, and IBM Quantum development tools.
  • Visualization & Web App: Streamlit and Plotly for interactive maps, hover details, and feature mismatch bar charts.
  • Hardware & Execution: Developed locally via Anaconda environments (run_all.py), validated through numerical simulations, and compiled for quantum circuit execution (including tests simulating noisy backend devices like FakeTorino via step6_hardware.py).

5. How is your project creative? QuantumAnalog introduces a novel intersection between quantum machine learning and planetary geology by adapting a mesh-of-cells approach from fluid dynamics and mapping multi-planetary surface parameters into quantum state spaces via 6-qubit fidelity kernels. Furthermore, its leave-one-feature-out anomaly attribution transforms abstract similarity scores into intuitive, actionable geological insights, establishing a rigorous framework for comparing classical and quantum models on real-world Earth-science data.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Physical Comparability: Enforcing a single pixel size, neighbourhood, and normalization rule across all three planetary bodies so comparisons remain physically meaningful rather than artifacts of resolution differences.
  • Honesty & Rigorous Benchmarking: Rejecting incomparable features (such as absolute temperature or elevation) and transparently benchmarking classical versus quantum kernels on Death Valley data, accounting for overlapping desert basin similarities.
  • Cost and Accessibility: Designing the pipeline to run entirely on free NASA data, free open-source software, laptop quantum simulators, and within IBM's free hardware tier.
dataRefs: earth_benchmark_death_valley/ - SRTMGL3 v003 tiles N35-N37, W116-W119: To benchmark Death Valley spatial terrain parameters.
earth_new_region_kharan/ - SRTMGL3 v003 tiles N27-N29, E062-E065: For mapping new Kharan-Chagai region analog.
earth_albedo/ - VIIRS VNP43C3 v002, 2023-07-01: Providing earth surface reflectance and albedo data.
mars/ - MOLA megt90n000fb.img + label; TES global_albedo_8ppd.img + label: Providing Martian topography and global albedo maps.
moon/ - LOLA LDEM_16.IMG + label; LDAM_10_FLOAT.IMG + label: Supplying lunar elevation models and reflectance data.
